questions.prompt: Which set of properties describes a typical metal?
options: Shiny, malleable, and a good conductor of heat and electricity
Dull, brittle, and a poor conductor
Colorless, odorless, and a gas at room temperature
questions.explanation: Metals are shiny (luster), malleable (hammered into sheets), and excellent conductors of heat and electricity.
questions.misconception: The dull, brittle, poor-conductor set belongs to nonmetals — the two families are opposites, and mixing their traits is a very common mix-up.

questions.prompt: Why do metals conduct electricity so well?
options: Their loose outer electrons can move freely through the metal
They are heavier than other elements
They store electricity inside their atoms
questions.explanation: Metal atoms release loose outer electrons that wander freely between atoms, and that moving charge IS the electric current.
questions.misconception: Weight and temperature have nothing to do with conduction — it is the free-moving electrons that let current flow, which is why nonmetals, with tightly held electrons, do not conduct.

questions.prompt: Where do metals sit on the periodic table?
options: On the left side and in the middle
questions.explanation: Metals fill the left side and the middle of the table — about 80% of all elements are metals.
questions.misconception: The right side of the table is where nonmetals live; the majority family — metals — owns the left and center.

questions.prompt: In reactions, what do metal atoms tend to do with their outer electrons?
options: Lose them and become positive ions
Gain extra electrons and become negative ions
Share them equally with every atom
questions.explanation: Metals tend to lose their loose outer electrons and become positive ions (cations) — which is how they bond with negative nonmetal ions.
questions.misconception: It's nonmetals that tend to gain electrons; metals do the opposite — giving theirs away — which is exactly why the two families pair up so well in ionic bonds.
